1170.title: Sudama's Handful of Rice
1170.hook: a poor friend hides a handful of rice from a king, and Vaisheshika names the unseen fruit of every deed
1170.carry: adrishta: every deed bears unseen fruit
1170.tomorrow: a mother asks her son what ends sorrow
1170.howItsDone: In the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition, adrishta is taught as the unseen result of past actions, and later thinkers such as Udayana argued that Ishvara guides it. Sudama's story is told at Krishna festivals, and at the Guruvayur temple in Kerala, on Kuchela Dinam, devotees offer flattened rice to Krishna in memory of him (Kuchela is his name in Malayalam tradition).

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika's list of substances ended with the self, known by the breath, and the mind, a gate for one thing at a time. Today, its last day, and its biggest idea.
screen: `ONE GATE, ONE THING.` · `VAISHESHIKA, A LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, a poor Brahmin, the one families know as Sudama, is told by his wife: you went to school with Krishna, and now he's king of Dvaraka. Go and see him. He has nothing to bring. So she begs a few handfuls of flattened rice from the neighbors and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to meet him and washes his feet. Sudama, ashamed, keeps the rice hidden. Krishna notices anyway, pulls the bundle free and eats a handful with delight: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, he says, offered with love, I accept. Sudama walks home without asking for a thing. Where his hut stood, he finds a palace.
screen: `A POOR FRIEND, A HANDFUL OF RICE.` → `HE HIDES IT.` → `KRISHNA EATS IT ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Vaisheshika has a word for what runs underneath that story: adrishta, the unseen. The Vaisheshika Sutra says the upward flaming of fire, the sideways blowing of wind, even the first motion of the atoms come from adrishta. In this school, every action leaves something behind that no one can see, merit, punya, or its opposite, and that residue keeps working until it bears fruit. This is the Hindu teaching of karma at its most physical: the deed is over, and its fruit is still on the way. Then a question. Who keeps track? Later Nyaya-Vaisheshika thinkers, Udayana among them, argued that the unseen needs a knower to guide it, and that the knower is Ishvara, God, who brings each deed to its fruit. Not every reader of the old Sutra sees God there; the school has room for that debate. But look at the story again. Sudama hid his gift. Krishna saw it. Sudama asked for nothing, and the fruit came anyway. It's one reason many Hindu families prize gupt daan, secret giving: an extra plate for a guest, a coin in the temple box, and no one told. Punya doesn't need an audience. And today, the kindness nobody noticed isn't lost. In Hindu terms, it's already moving.
screen: `ADRISHTA: WHY FIRE RISES.` · `EVERY DEED LEAVES PUNYA, OR ITS OPPOSITE.` · `UDAYANA: ISHVARA GUIDES THE UNSEEN.` · `SUDAMA HID HIS GIFT.` · then, large: `THE FRUIT IS ON THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Sit for a couple of minutes and bring to mind one thing you did yesterday that nobody saw: a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or dropped. Don't judge it; just notice that it isn't finished, that something of it is still moving. If you pray, you can offer that deed to Krishna, or the name of God you use, the way Sudama's rice was offered. If you don't, simply hold it, and let it be seen by you.

1171.title: Kapila Teaches His Mother
1171.hook: Devahuti asks her son Kapila to end her sorrow, and Samkhya begins with three kinds of pain
1171.carry: three kinds of pain, and knowing ends them
1171.howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and taught alongside Yoga, its paired school. Kapila's teaching to Devahuti fills chapters of the Bhagavata's third book, and many Hindus close prayers with Om shanti, shanti, shanti, often explained as peace from the three kinds of pain.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika closed with adrishta: Sudama's hidden rice, and the unseen fruit of every deed. A new school opens today, with a mother and her son.
screen: `ADRISHTA: THE UNSEEN FRUIT.` · `A NEW SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana, a woman named Devahuti has spent long years serving a sage, Kardama. When their son is born, the sage, his promise kept, leaves for the forest. Devahuti is left at home with the boy, Kapila. And she knows something about him: the Bhagavata says he is Vishnu himself, come to teach. So one day she sits before her own son and asks for help. I'm tired, she says, of senses that never stop wanting. They've pulled me into the dark. You're the light I need. Cut through this confusion. A mother asking her child for wisdom. Kapila smiles, and begins.
screen: `A MOTHER ASKS HER SON.` → `END MY CONFUSION.` → `KAPILA SMILES.`

segments.voice: Tradition names Kapila as the source of Samkhya, the school that opens today. The Bhagavata's Kapila teaches it with love of God at the center; the school's oldest surviving book, Ishvarakrishna's Samkhya Karika, sets it out on its own. Both start where Devahuti started: with pain. The Karika's first verse says: because we're struck by three kinds of pain, we want to know what ends it. Commentators sort them: pain from within, in body and mind; pain from other beings; and pain from forces beyond us. Then an objector asks: why philosophy? There's medicine. The Karika doesn't call medicine bad. It says the seen remedies aren't certain and aren't final; the pain comes back. Even rituals, it says, help but wear off. What ends pain is knowing: what's manifest, what's unmanifest, and the knower. In the Bhagavata, Kapila tells his mother the same thing in his own way: the mind is what binds and what frees. Caught in the world's three strands, it binds; turned toward the Lord, it frees. And you've heard this teaching before. When Hindus close a prayer with Om shanti, shanti, shanti, many teachers explain the three as peace from those same three kinds of pain: from within, from others, from the world. So the doctor and the medicine are real, and Samkhya keeps them. It just says the deepest peace comes from seeing clearly who is suffering.
screen: `SAMKHYA, FROM KAPILA.` · `THREE KINDS OF PAIN.` · `KNOW THE WORLD, AND THE KNOWER.` · `OM SHANTI, SHANTI, SHANTI.` · then, large: `KNOWING ENDS IT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one pain you're carrying and simply sort it: from within, from another person, or from the world. Then, if you pray, say Om shanti, shanti, shanti softly, one shanti for each kind, the way many Hindus close a prayer. If you don't pray, name each kind and let one long breath out after it. If a pain is ever too heavy, or you think of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

1172.title: Two Birds on One Tree
1172.hook: two birds on one tree, one eating and one watching: Samkhya's purusha and prakriti
1172.carry: purusha, the witness, is not the worry
1172.howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and its map of purusha and prakriti is taught alongside the Yoga Sutras, which build on it. The two-birds verse is often taught in Hindu study groups, and resting as the witness, sakshi bhava, is a practice many teachers give.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Samkhya began with Devahuti's question and three kinds of pain. Today, its first two.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF PAIN.` · `SAMKHYA'S FIRST TWO.`

segments.voice: There's a picture so old it's in the Rig Veda, and the Upanishads keep it. Two birds, close friends, sit on the same tree. One hops from branch to branch, eating the fruit, sweet and bitter, and every bite changes its mood. The other eats nothing. It just looks on. The Mundaka Upanishad adds the turn: the eating bird, sunk in its troubles, grieves, until it looks up and sees the other one, the Lord, calm and content. Then its grief falls away. Same tree, same branch, two very different birds.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, ONE TREE.` → `ONE EATS, ONE WATCHES.` → `IT LOOKS UP.`

segments.voice: Samkhya reads the picture in its own terms. The tree, the fruit, the hunger and every mood a bite brings belong to prakriti. The Samkhya Karika calls prakriti the root, not made by anything; everything else unfolds out of it. Mountains, yes, and your body. But here's the surprise: your senses, your mind, your thoughts, even your sense of being an I, sit on prakriti's side too. In Samkhya, a worry is as much part of nature as a cloud. The watching one is purusha. The Karika describes it in a short string of words: a witness, a seer, neutral, standing apart, not the doer. Purusha doesn't think the thoughts; they show up before it. The eating bird's grief, in Samkhya's reading, is a mix-up: the witness taking nature's moods as its own. Here the schools part ways, and Hindus let them. The Upanishad, as you heard, calls the watching bird the Lord. Advaita Vedanta, still to come, reads the self as one. The Karika counts many witnesses, one for each of us, and leaves God out of its count. But they share a teaching Hindus come back to again and again: you are not only the bird that eats. Many teachers call resting there sakshi bhava, being the witness. Today, the dread before a test is real fruit on the tree. It isn't the one watching.
screen: `PRAKRITI: THE TREE, THE FRUIT, THE MOOD.` · `PURUSHA: THE WITNESS.` · `THE SCHOOLS PART WAYS.` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT ONLY THE BIRD THAT EATS.`

segments.voice: For a couple of minutes, let things show up: a sound from the street, an itch, a thought about tomorrow. Each time, don't push it away and don't follow it; just note, quietly, seen, as if from the branch above. That's sakshi bhava, resting as the witness. If you pray, you can let a prayer be one more thing that rises and is seen. If you don't, the noting is the whole practice.
Samkhya. The school that starts its count with two: prakriti, the tree, the fruit and every mood, and purusha, the one who watches.

1173.title: Krishna and the Three Strands
1173.hook: Arjuna asks Krishna how to spot someone free of the three gunas, and the answer reaches the kitchen
1173.carry: the three gunas weave every mood and meal
1173.tomorrow: the gods win a battle, and a blade of grass
1173.howItsDone: Many Hindu teachers use the three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, to speak about food, moods and habits, following the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14 and 17). Many families keep puja and fast-day food sattvic, and some leave out onion and garlic, a later custom built on the same idea.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Samkhya: two birds on one tree, purusha the witness and prakriti everything it sees. Today, what prakriti is made of.
screen: `TWO BIRDS, ONE TREE.` · `PRAKRITI'S THREE STRANDS.`

segments.voice: Two armies wait. In the chariot between them, Krishna is teaching Arjuna, and in the fourteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita he names three forces, born of nature, that tie every embodied being to the world. Arjuna, a practical man, asks the practical question: how would I recognize someone who has gone beyond them? How do they act? Krishna's answer surprises. That person, he says, doesn't hate clarity, or restless activity, or even confusion when it comes, and doesn't long for any of them when it goes. They sit like someone looking on, and know: it's only the strands, moving.
screen: `ARJUNA ASKS: HOW WOULD I KNOW THEM?` → `THEY DON'T HATE THE HEAVY DAY.` → `ONLY THE STRANDS, MOVING.`

segments.voice: Those three are the gunas, and Samkhya puts them at the heart of prakriti. Guna is often translated strand or quality. The Samkhya Karika describes them in a single verse. Sattva is light, and shows things: the morning every page lands. Rajas stirs and moves: the morning you check your phone, refill your water and plan the whole semester. Tamas is heavy, and covers: the paragraph you read four times. Everything on prakriti's side, a stone, a meal, a mood, is some mix of the three. They aren't heroes and villains. The Karika says they lean on one another and take turns on top, working together the way a lamp does; commentators spell it out as oil, wick and flame making one light. And this teaching lives in Hindu kitchens. In the Gita's seventeenth chapter, Krishna sorts food by the gunas: wholesome, pleasing food that brings long life, strength and cheer is dear to the sattvic; food too bitter, sour, salty or burning, to the rajasic; stale, leftover food, to the tamasic. That's why many Hindu families speak of a sattvic meal, and why many cook without onion and garlic for puja or on fast days, a later custom that counts those two as stirring or heavy. It lives in hard mornings too. Krishna's free person doesn't hate the heavy day. She knows it's the strands, and strands take turns.
screen: `PRAKRITI HAS THREE STRANDS.` · `SATTVA, RAJAS, TAMAS.` · `ONE LAMP: OIL, WICK, FLAME.` · `GITA 17: FOOD HAS GUNAS TOO.` · then, large: `THE STRANDS TAKE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Check in with what's here right now: something restless, an urge to move or plan; something heavy, a fog or a pull toward sleep; something clear. No score; just notice the mix, and that it shifts. Then, at your next meal, pause before the first bite. Many Hindus offer the food first, some with the Gita's verse that begins brahmarpanam. If you pray, offer the plate in your own words. If you don't, simply look at it with thanks.
Samkhya. The school that sees prakriti woven from three gunas: sattva, clear; rajas, moving; tamas, heavy. Together, like oil, wick and flame, they make one light.

1174.howItsDone: Students of Samkhya, and of the Yoga traditions that use its map, learn the unfolding of prakriti in order, from buddhi and ahamkara down to the elements. Many Hindus close a puja or a day's work by offering it to God, often with words like Sri Krishnarpanamastu.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Samkhya: the three gunas, which Krishna told Arjuna weave everything, even a meal.
screen: `THE THREE GUNAS.` · `THEY WEAVE EVEN A MEAL.`

segments.voice: The Kena Upanishad tells it. The gods win a great battle, and they celebrate: our victory, our greatness. Then a strange being appears before them, and no one can say what it is. Agni, the god of fire, goes to find out. Who are you? it asks. I'm Agni. I can burn up everything on earth. The being sets down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushes at it with all his force, and can't. Vayu, the wind, tries next: I can carry off anything on earth. The grass doesn't move. Then Indra goes, and the being vanishes. In its place stands a shining goddess, Uma. That, she tells him, was Brahman. The victory was Brahman's. You were the ones boasting.
screen: `OUR VICTORY!` → `ONE BLADE OF GRASS.` → `IT WAS NEVER YOURS ALONE.`

segments.voice: Samkhya has a precise name for the gods' mistake, and puts it in a surprising place. The Samkhya Karika lays out the order of unfolding. From prakriti, the root, comes mahat, the great one, also called buddhi. Buddhi is marked by deciding: this, not that. From buddhi comes ahamkara, marked by the claim of I. Translators often render it ego, or the I-maker. It's the reflex that says our victory, my idea, my turn, before anyone checks. Notice the order: in Samkhya, deciding and the sense of me unfold before earth and water. And notice the side of the line. Buddhi and ahamkara both belong to prakriti. They're instruments, finely made, but not purusha, the witness. The Bhagavad Gita puts it in one line: all actions are done by the gunas of prakriti, but the one confused by ahamkara thinks, I am the doer. Hindus act on that teaching every day. After a puja, a meal or a day's work, many say a short line that hands it over: Krishnarpanam, to Krishna; and at the sacred fire, idam na mama, this is not mine. Hindu schools explain the self in different ways, and they'll have their say. But in Samkhya, the I-maker is a tool, and tools can be noticed. Today, when something goes well, ask the question Uma answered for Indra: whose victory is it?
screen: `ROOT, THEN BUDDHI: IT DECIDES.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `BOTH ON NATURE'S SIDE.` · `GITA 3.27: "I AM THE DOER."` · then, large: `WHOSE VICTORY IS IT?`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that went well this week: a grade, a meal, a kind word. Notice how fast the tag arrives: I did that. Then trace it outward: the teacher who explained, the hands that grew the food, the breath that came on its own. If you pray, close by offering it, the way many Hindus do: Krishnarpanam, or the name of God you use. If you don't, just say quietly: not only mine.
Samkhya. Its map unfolds from the root: first buddhi, which decides, then ahamkara, which says I. Both on nature's side of the line.

1175.title: The Field and Its Knower

1175.howItsDone: Some students of Samkhya memorize the list of principles, the tattvas, from prakriti down to the elements, and teachers in Samkhya and Yoga lineages use it as a map for contemplation. The thirteenth chapter of the Gita, on the field and its knower, is often read and taught in Hindu study circles.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday in Samkhya: buddhi, which decides, and ahamkara, the I-maker. The gods boasted, and the grass wouldn't burn.
screen: `BUDDHI AND AHAMKARA.` · `THE GRASS WOULDN'T BURN.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavad Gita's first line names a place: the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus. Kurukshetra, a battlefield, where two armies wait. Twelve chapters later, Krishna takes that word and turns it on Arjuna himself. This body, he says, is called the field. And the one who knows it is called the knower of the field. Then he lists what's in the field, item by item, like someone walking a farm with a clipboard. A warrior standing on a field learns he's standing on two fields at once.
screen: `KURUKSHETRA: A FIELD.` → `THIS BODY IS A FIELD.` → `WHO KNOWS THE FIELD?`

segments.voice: Krishna's list is close to Samkhya's inventory. The Samkhya Karika sorts everything with one question: is it made, and does it make? The root, prakriti, makes but isn't made. Seven are made and making: buddhi, which decides; ahamkara, the I-maker; and five subtle elements, the bare potentials of sound, touch, form, taste and smell. Sixteen are made and make nothing more. Ten are organs: five take in the world, ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose; five act on it, speech, hands, feet, and the organs of release and of birth. One is manas, the mind, which shares in both, turning what comes in into a plan. And five are the elements you can stub your toe on: space, air, fire, water, earth. One root, seven, sixteen: the twenty-four principles. Krishna's field names many of the same: the great elements, ahamkara, buddhi, the unmanifest, the ten senses and the one. Then the Karika names one more, set apart from the list: purusha, neither made nor making: in the Gita's words, the knower of the field. Here Krishna adds what the Karika doesn't: know me, he says, as the knower in every field. That's the Hindu teaching of the field and its knower. Body, mind, even the I: the field, tended and changing. You are not only the field. Today, when your body's tired or your mind won't settle, walk the field like that farmer, and remember who's doing the knowing.
screen: `ONE QUESTION: MADE, OR MAKING?` · `ONE ROOT, SEVEN, SIXTEEN.` · `THE FIELD: BODY, MIND, EVEN THE I.` · `PURUSHA: THE KNOWER OF THE FIELD.` · then, large: `YOU ARE NOT ONLY THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly through the field of your own body: hearing, touch where your weight lands, seeing even with eyes closed, tasting, smelling; then your hands, your feet, your voice at rest, and the mind, already making plans. Each one is on the list. Then rest, and let the one who's been noticing it all stay unnamed. If you pray, you can close by greeting the one Krishna calls the knower in every field. If you don't, simply rest in the noticing.
Samkhya. Its inventory: one root, seven made and making, sixteen made only. Twenty-four principles, the field, and purusha, its knower, outside the list.

1176.hook: a wandering teacher wins over a king with a hundred teachers, and the king stays king

1176.howItsDone: The Samkhya Karika is read verse by verse with classical commentaries such as Gaudapada's, and its arguments, like the one for purusha, are studied alongside other schools' replies. Janaka is held up in Hindu teaching as the model of a householder who seeks freedom without leaving the world.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-ONE-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Samkhya's whole count got names: Krishna's field, twenty-four principles, and the knower outside the list.
screen: `KRISHNA'S FIELD.` · `TWENTY-FOUR, AND THE KNOWER.`

segments.voice: In the Mahabharata's great book of teachings, King Janaka of Mithila keeps a hundred teachers at his court, each with a different path to offer. Then a wandering teacher arrives: Panchashikha, a student in the line of the sage Kapila. He sits with the king's scholars and takes on their views one by one. And Janaka, the story says, sets aside his hundred teachers and follows this one. But he doesn't leave his throne. Janaka stays king. And in the same book he's remembered for one line: if Mithila burns, nothing of mine burns.
screen: `A HUNDRED TEACHERS.` → `ONE WANDERER FROM KAPILA'S LINE.` → `THE KING STAYS KING.`

segments.voice: Panchashikha's line is the one the Samkhya Karika names near its end: the teaching passed from Kapila to Asuri, from Asuri to Panchashikha, and down a line of students to Ishvarakrishna, who set it in these verses. And the Karika takes on the hardest question Janaka's court could ask. Purusha never acts. It doesn't think or move. So how could anyone know it's there? The Karika's first reason is homely: whatever is put together exists for someone else. Commentators make it concrete with a bed: frame, slats, mattress, all fitted together, and plainly for a sleeper who isn't one of the parts. Now look at a body and a mind, all fitted together. For whom? The verse adds more: there must be something beyond the three gunas, someone to oversee it all, someone who experiences it; and people strive for release, which makes no sense unless someone is there to be freed. Samkhya can't point at purusha. It infers it, the way you'd infer a sleeper from a made bed. Then Janaka shows what the knowing is for. Hindus hold him up as the householder sage, free while ruling a city, and the Bhagavad Gita names him: Janaka and others reached perfection through action. So in Hindu teaching, you don't have to leave home for the forest to be free. A job, a family and a full calendar aren't in the way. They're the bed. Remember who it's made for.
screen: `KAPILA, ASURI, PANCHASHIKHA, ISHVARAKRISHNA.` · `WHAT'S PUT TOGETHER IS FOR ANOTHER.` · `INFERRED, NOT POINTED AT.` · `GITA 3.20: JANAKA, THROUGH ACTION.` · then, large: `FREE WHILE LIVING IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Notice the arrangement you are right now: the spine holding you up, the lungs filling, the heart keeping time, the ears taking in the room. Feel the whole assembly at once, and rest in the plain fact that it's being experienced. Then think of one duty waiting for you today, and plan to do it the way Janaka ruled: fully, without being owned by it. If you pray, give thanks for the body that's been made, and offer the day's work in your own words.
The Samkhya Karika. Ishvarakrishna's verses, from Kapila's line, which reason that whatever is put together, like a bed, is for someone outside it: purusha.
